claim: Phytoplankton-bacteria interactions drive the surface ocean sulfur cycle and local climatic processes through the production and exchange of dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP).
source: Phytoplankton-bacteria interactions drive the surface ocean sulfur cycle and local climatic processes through the production and exchange of a key compound: dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP).
evidence: This is a general statement about the role of DMSP in ocean sulfur cycling and climate, drawing from established scientific understanding.

claim: This study provides the first visualization of DMSP at sub-cellular levels using secondary-ion mass spectrometry.
source: Here we use secondary-ion mass spectrometry to provide the first visualization of DMSP at sub-cellular levels, tracking the fate of a stable sulfur isotope (34S) from its incorporation by microalgae as inorganic sulfate to its biosynthesis and exudation as DMSP, and finally its uptake and degradation by bacteria.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodology and results of using SIMS to visualize DMSP at subcellular resolution.

claim: DMSP storage locations in microalgae include vacuoles, cytoplasm and chloroplasts, with high enrichments present in these organelles.
source: Our results identify for the first time the storage locations of DMSP in microalgae, with high enrichments present in vacuoles, cytoplasm and chloroplasts.
evidence: This claim is supported by NanoSIMS data showing 34S enrichment in specific cellular compartments.

claim: DMSP-degrading bacteria contain seven times more 34S than the control strain at the single-cell level.
source: In addition, we quantify DMSP incorporation at the single-cell level, with DMSP-degrading bacteria containing seven times more 34S than the control strain.
evidence: This is quantified by NanoSIMS measurements comparing Pseudovibrio sp. and E. coli.

claim: Interactions between marine phytoplankton and bacteria control chemical cycling and energy transfer to higher trophic levels.
source: Interactions between marine phytoplankton and bacteria constitute an important ecological linkage in the oceans (Cole, 1982), controlling chemical cycling and energy transfer to higher trophic levels (Azam and Malfatti, 2007; Falkowski et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The cycling of sulfur depends on metabolic interactions between phytoplankton and bacteria.
source: The cycling of sulfur, an essential element for living organisms, depends on the metabolic interactions between these two Kingdoms (Sievert et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sievert et al., 2007.

claim: DMSP is produced by phytoplankton and degraded by marine bacteria and phytoplankton themselves into dimethylsulfide (DMS).
source: A striking example is the production of the sulfur compound dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP) by phytoplankton and its degradation by marine bacteria (and phytoplankton themselves) into the climate-active gas dimethylsulfide (DMS) (Alcolombri et al., 2015; Ayers and Gras, 1991; Howard et al., 2006; Todd et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: DMS release into the atmosphere contributes 90% of biogenic sulfur emissions.
source: The subsequent release of DMS into the atmosphere contributes 90% of biogenic sulfur emissions and initiates the formation and growth of aerosols, thereby enhancing cloud formation and sunlight scattering (Ayers and Gras, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ayers and Gras, 1991.

claim: DMS initiates the formation and growth of aerosols, thereby enhancing cloud formation and sunlight scattering.
source: The subsequent release of DMS into the atmosphere contributes 90% of biogenic sulfur emissions and initiates the formation and growth of aerosols, thereby enhancing cloud formation and sunlight scattering (Ayers and Gras, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ayers and Gras, 1991.

claim: Chemical interactions between marine microorganisms at micrometre-scales can have large-scale impacts on climate.
source: This highlights how chemical interactions occurring between marine microorganisms across micrometre-scales can ultimately have large-scale impacts on climate (Sievert et al., 2007; Simó, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Direct measurements of metabolic interactions critical to global sulfur cycling have not previously been possible at the sub-cellular level.
source: However, direct measurements of these metabolic interactions, critical to the global sulfur cycling, have not previously been possible at the scale where they occur, the sub-cellular level.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study's approach.

claim: In the surface ocean, the largest quantities of sulfur are present as dissolved sulfate, which constitutes the main sulfur source for phytoplankton.
source: In the surface ocean, the largest quantities of sulfur are present as dissolved sulfate, which constitutes the main sulfur source for phytoplankton (Sievert et al., 2007; Stefels, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Most sulfur derived from sulfate uptake is converted by phytoplankton into sulfur-based amino acids, and a fraction is used to synthesise DMSP.
source: Most of the sulfur derived from sulfate uptake is converted by these organisms into sulfur-based amino acids, and a fraction is ultimately used to synthesise DMSP (Stefels, 2000) (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Globally, more than a billion tons of DMSP are produced every year.
source: Globally, more than a billion tons of DMSP are produced every year, which has been estimated to represent up to 10% of the amount of carbon fixed by phytoplankton (Archer et al., 2001; Simó et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: DMSP production represents up to 10% of the amount of carbon fixed by phytoplankton.
source: Globally, more than a billion tons of DMSP are produced every year, which has been estimated to represent up to 10% of the amount of carbon fixed by phytoplankton (Archer et al., 2001; Simó et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous studies in higher plants provided strong evidence that DMSP biosynthesis starts in the cytosol and ends in the chloroplast.
source: Previous studies in higher plants provided strong evidence that DMSP biosynthesis starts in the cytosol and ends in the chloroplast (Trossat et al., 1996, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: DMSP biosynthesis occurs through a different route in phytoplankton compared to higher plants.
source: However, DMSP biosynthesis occur through a different route in phytoplankton (Stefels, 2000), and we still do not know: (1) where this compound is produced and stored in phytoplankton cells; (2) what are its functions; and (3) how efficiently it is transferred from phytoplankton producers to bacterial degraders.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stefels, 2000.

claim: The location where DMSP is produced and stored in phytoplankton cells was previously unknown.
source: However, DMSP biosynthesis occur through a different route in phytoplankton (Stefels, 2000), and we still do not know: (1) where this compound is produced and stored in phytoplankton cells; (2) what are its functions; and (3) how efficiently it is transferred from phytoplankton producers to bacterial degraders.
evidence: This is a statement about the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Symbiodinium is a taxon that includes some of the most prodigious DMSP producers on the planet.
source: We used the dinoflagellate Symbiodinium, a taxon that includes some of the most prodigious DMSP producers on the planet (Caruana and Malin, 2014; Saltzman and Cooper, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Symbiodinium cells can be free-living in the water column or form endosymbiotic associations with tropical cnidarians.
source: Symbiodinium cells can be free-living in the water column, but are primarily known for the endosymbiotic associations they form with tropical cnidarians that fuel the extremely high productivity of coral reef ecosystems (Dubinsky, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dubinsky, 1990.

claim: Populations of reef-building corals are major DMSP production hotspots.
source: Populations of reef-building corals are major DMSP production hotspots (Broadbent et al., 2002; Raina et al., 2013) and their contribution to the marine sulfur cycle is disproportionately large given their relatively restricted distributions (Raina et al., 2013; Fischer and Jones, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Coral contribution to the marine sulfur cycle is disproportionately large given their relatively restricted distributions.
source: Populations of reef-building corals are major DMSP production hotspots (Broadbent et al., 2002; Raina et al., 2013) and their contribution to the marine sulfur cycle is disproportionately large given their relatively restricted distributions (Raina et al., 2013; Fischer and Jones, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: DMSP constitutes an important source of carbon and sulfur for bacterial communities harboured by corals.
source: In this ecosystem, DMSP constitutes an important source of carbon and sulfur for the diverse and highly abundant bacterial communities harboured by corals (Raina et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Raina et al., 2010.

claim: Symbiodinium cells were incubated for 18 days in artificial seawater containing 34S-labelled sulfate as the sole sulfur source.
source: Symbiodinium cells were incubated for 18 days in artificial seawater containing 34S-labelled sulfate as the sole sulfur source (34S-ASW; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: All Symbiodinium cultures were rinsed thoroughly and re-inoculated into ASW containing sulfate in natural isotopic abundance before addition of bacterial cells to prevent direct uptake of 34S-sulfate by bacteria.
source: To prevent direct uptake of 34S-sulfate by bacteria, all Symbiodinium cultures were rinsed thoroughly and re-inoculated into ASW containing sulfate in natural isotopic abundance (natS-ASW) before addition of bacterial cells.
evidence: This describes a methodological step to ensure that bacteria only take up 34S from DMSP, not from sulfate.

claim: Pseudovibrio sp. P12 is a DMSP-degrading bacterium isolated from healthy corals.
source: Two different bacterial strains were added to the rinsed cultures and co-incubated for six hours: (i) Pseudovibrio sp. P12, a DMSP-degrading bacterium isolated from healthy corals (Raina et al., 2016), selected because of its worldwide distribution in coastal waters (Shieh et al., 2004) and its abundance in benthic invertebrate communities (Bondarev et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Pseudovibrio sp. P12 has a worldwide distribution in coastal waters.
source: Two different bacterial strains were added to the rinsed cultures and co-incubated for six hours: (i) Pseudovibrio sp. P12, a DMSP-degrading bacterium isolated from healthy corals (Raina et al., 2016), selected because of its worldwide distribution in coastal waters (Shieh et al., 2004) and its abundance in benthic invertebrate communities (Bondarev et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shieh et al., 2004.

claim: Pseudovibrio sp. P12 is abundant in benthic invertebrate communities.
source: Two different bacterial strains were added to the rinsed cultures and co-incubated for six hours: (i) Pseudovibrio sp. P12, a DMSP-degrading bacterium isolated from healthy corals (Raina et al., 2016), selected because of its worldwide distribution in coastal waters (Shieh et al., 2004) and its abundance in benthic invertebrate communities (Bondarev et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bondarev et al., 2013.

claim: Escherichia coli W (ATCC 9637) is able to grow in seawater and not capable of degrading DMSP.
source: and (ii) a control, Escherichia coli W (ATCC 9637), a widely studied and fully sequenced strain, able to grow in seawater and not capable of degrading DMSP.
evidence: This describes the properties of the control bacterial strain used in the study.

claim: Both bacterial strains were pre-grown in a medium enriched in the rare stable isotope 15N to precisely localise bacterial cells.
source: To precisely localise bacterial cells, both strains were pre-grown in a medium enriched in the rare stable isotope 15N (in amino-acids and ammonium form).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology for labeling bacteria.

claim: Cellular incorporation of stable isotope tracers (34S and 15N) was identified by an increase in the sulfur (34S/32S) and/or nitrogen (15N/14N) ratio above their natural abundance values (0.043 and 0.0037, respectively).
source: The cellular incorporation of the stable isotope tracers (34S and 15N) was identified by an increase in the sulfur (34S/32S) and/or nitrogen (15N/14N) ratio above their natural abundance values (0.043 and 0.0037, respectively).
evidence: This describes the analytical approach for detecting isotope incorporation.

claim: Symbiodinium cell numbers doubled during the incubation period in the medium containing 34S-labelled sulfate, reaching approximately 2.9 million cells ml−1 after 18 days.
source: Symbiodinium cell numbers doubled during the incubation period in the medium containing 34S-labelled sulfate, reaching approximately 2.9 million cells ml−1 after 18 days (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: LC-MS analyses confirmed that all cultures initially incubated with 34S-sulfate were highly enriched in 34S-DMSP, which represented up to 46% of the DMSP molecules present in samples analysed.
source: LC-MS analyses carried out at the end of the experiment on extracted Symbiodinium cells confirmed that all cultures initially incubated with 34S-sulfate were highly enriched in 34S-DMSP, which represented up to 46% of the DMSP molecules present in samples analysed (Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 2 and source data.

claim: Sulfur atoms used by dinoflagellates to synthesise DMSP can originate from the uptake of inorganic sulfate derived from seawater.
source: This result confirms that sulfur atoms used by dinoflagellates to synthesise DMSP can originate from the uptake of inorganic sulfate derived from seawater (Stefels, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by the LC-MS data showing 34S incorporation into DMSP, and a citation to Stefels, 2000.

claim: High levels of 32S-DMSP (ranging from 54% to 66% of total DMSP) were recorded in Symbiodinium cultures in addition to 34S-DMSP.
source: In addition to 34S-DMSP, unexpectedly high levels of 32S-DMSP (ranging from 54% to 66% of total DMSP) were recorded in Symbiodinium cultures (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: The presence of high levels of 32S-DMSP can be explained by Symbiodinium cells retaining a large fraction of the natural pool of 32S initially present in the starting culture and by new 32S-DMSP being synthesised during the six hours in natS-ASW medium.
source: The presence of these high levels of 32S-DMSP can be explained by a combination of two factors: (i) Symbiodinium cells density only doubled during the incubation phase in 34S-ASW, retaining a large fraction of the natural pool of 32S initially present in the starting culture prior to the incubation; (ii) new 32S-DMSP might have been synthesised during the six hours immediately preceding sampling, when Symbiodinium cells were incubated in natS-ASW medium.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and observed data.

claim: Sulfur containing amino acids (methionine and cysteine) were not detected by LC-MS or 1H NMR in Symbiodinium extracts.
source: Although high concentrations of DMSP were present in the methanolic Symbiodinium cells extract (Figure 2—source data 1), sulfur containing amino acids (methionine and cysteine) were not detected by LC-MS or 1H NMR.
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of detection in analytical measurements.

claim: The entire sampling procedure leading to SIMS analyses had to be water-free to effectively prevent the loss of DMSP from the cells.
source: To effectively prevent the loss of DMSP from the cells, the entire sampling procedure leading to SIMS analyses had to be water-free, with all steps performed under strict anhydrous conditions.
evidence: This describes a methodological requirement for preserving DMSP in samples.

claim: Cryopreservation techniques followed by freeze substitution in an acrolein-ether mixture were used to preserve DMSP in cells.
source: For this, we used cryopreservation techniques followed by freeze substitution in an acrolein-ether mixture.
evidence: This describes the sample preparation methodology.

claim: The acrolein-ether freeze substitution method has routinely been used to successfully preserve cellular ions and compounds in a variety of systems.
source: This method has routinely been used to successfully preserve cellular ions and compounds in a variety of systems (Altus and Canny, 1985; Ashford et al., 1999; Kaiser et al., 2015; Marshall et al., 2007; Mostaert et al., 1996), with the acrolein stabilizing and preserving cellular proteins, nucleic and fatty acids through cross linking, while the low temperature, anhydrous conditions ensure preservation and retention of diffusible ions and water-soluble molecules (such as DMSP).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Acrolein stabilizes and preserves cellular proteins, nucleic and fatty acids through cross linking.
source: This method has routinely been used to successfully preserve cellular ions and compounds in a variety of systems (Altus and Canny, 1985; Ashford et al., 1999; Kaiser et al., 2015; Marshall et al., 2007; Mostaert et al., 1996), with the acrolein stabilizing and preserving cellular proteins, nucleic and fatty acids through cross linking, while the low temperature, anhydrous conditions ensure preservation and retention of diffusible ions and water-soluble molecules (such as DMSP).
evidence: This describes the mechanism by which acrolein preserves cellular components.

claim: Low temperature, anhydrous conditions ensure preservation and retention of diffusible ions and water-soluble molecules such as DMSP.
source: This method has routinely been used to successfully preserve cellular ions and compounds in a variety of systems (Altus and Canny, 1985; Ashford et al., 1999; Kaiser et al., 2015; Marshall et al., 2007; Mostaert et al., 1996), with the acrolein stabilizing and preserving cellular proteins, nucleic and fatty acids through cross linking, while the low temperature, anhydrous conditions ensure preservation and retention of diffusible ions and water-soluble molecules (such as DMSP).
evidence: This describes the mechanism by which the preservation method retains DMSP.

claim: The inclusion of acrolein ensures excellent cell structural preservation at a low temperature, which is required for high resolution NanoSIMS analyses.
source: The inclusion of acrolein ensures excellent cell structural preservation at a low temperature, which is required for high resolution NanoSIMS analyses (Kaiser et al., 2015; Marshall, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ToF-SIMS revealed that 34S-DMSP was present and abundant in the preserved cells following resin embedding, with a ratio of 34S-DMSP/32S-DMSP matching the bulk analyses carried out with LC-MS prior to embedding.
source: ToF-SIMS revealed that 34S-DMSP was present and abundant in the preserved cells following resin embedding, with a ratio of 34S-DMSP/32S-DMSP matching the bulk analyses carried out with LC-MS prior to embedding (Figure 2c–d, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ToF-SIMS data shown in Figure 2.

claim: NanoSIMS analysis revealed that Symbiodinium exposed to 34S-labelled sulfate were nine times more enriched in 34S than the cells in the control.
source: NanoSIMS analysis revealed that Symbiodinium exposed to 34S-labelled sulfate were nine times more enriched in 34S than the cells in the control (34S/32S ratio in 34S-ASW treatments: 0.391 ± 0.046, compared to natS-ASW controls 0.044 ± 0.001 [Figure 4—figure supplement 1]).
evidence: This claim is supported by NanoSIMS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Substantial spatial variability in 34S enrichment was detected within Symbiodinium cells.
source: Furthermore, substantial spatial variability in 34S enrichment was detected within Symbiodinium cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by NanoSIMS imaging data showing different enrichment levels in different cellular compartments.

claim: Relatively low level of 34S enrichments were detected in the nucleus (34S/32S: 0.087 ± 0.004).
source: Relatively low level of enrichments were detected in the nucleus (34S/32S: 0.087 ± 0.004) which might correspond to the presence of 34S-labelled amino-acids in the histone-like proteins that condense Symbiodinium DNA into chromosomes (Shoguchi et al., 2013) (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by NanoSIMS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Low 34S enrichment in the nucleus might correspond to the presence of 34S-labelled amino-acids in the histone-like proteins that condense Symbiodinium DNA into chromosomes.
source: Relatively low level of enrichments were detected in the nucleus (34S/32S: 0.087 ± 0.004) which might correspond to the presence of 34S-labelled amino-acids in the histone-like proteins that condense Symbiodinium DNA into chromosomes (Shoguchi et al., 2013) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the NanoSIMS data and knowledge of Symbiodinium biology.

claim: Much higher 34S enrichment levels were detected in vacuoles (34S/32S: 0.337 ± 0.011), chloroplasts (34S/32S: 0.384 ± 0.020) and cytoplasm (34S/32S: 0.451 ± 0.025).
source: Much higher enrichment levels were detected in vacuoles (34S/32S: 0.337 ± 0.011), chloroplasts (34S/32S: 0.384 ± 0.020) and cytoplasm (34S/32S: 0.451 ± 0.025); which means that the enrichment in these cellular structures was 7.7, 8.8 and 10.3 times over the natural abundance levels (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by NanoSIMS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The enrichment in vacuoles, chloroplasts and cytoplasm was 7.7, 8.8 and 10.3 times over the natural abundance levels, respectively.
source: Much higher enrichment levels were detected in vacuoles (34S/32S: 0.337 ± 0.011), chloroplasts (34S/32S: 0.384 ± 0.020) and cytoplasm (34S/32S: 0.451 ± 0.025); which means that the enrichment in these cellular structures was 7.7, 8.8 and 10.3 times over the natural abundance levels (Figure 3).
evidence: This is calculated from the NanoSIMS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The largest 34S enrichment was observed in small hotspots often observed near the Symbiodinium cell periphery (34S/32S: 0.971 ± 0.059), reaching more than 22 times the natural abundance level.
source: However, the largest 34S enrichment was observed in small hotspots often observed near the Symbiodinium cell periphery (34S/32S: 0.971 ± 0.059; Figure 3), reaching more than 22 times the natural abundance level.
evidence: This claim is supported by NanoSIMS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The hotspots with high 34S enrichment are likely storage droplets containing sulfolipids based on their small size and high 34S enrichment.
source: Based on their small size and their high 34S enrichment, these hotpots are likely storage droplets containing sulfolipids, a group of sulfur compounds known to accumulate in Symbiodinium (Garrett et al., 2013; Yuyama et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the NanoSIMS data and citations to previous research on sulfolipids in Symbiodinium.

claim: Sulfolipids are a group of sulfur compounds known to accumulate in Symbiodinium.
source: Based on their small size and their high 34S enrichment, these hotpots are likely storage droplets containing sulfolipids, a group of sulfur compounds known to accumulate in Symbiodinium (Garrett et al., 2013; Yuyama et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Lipid droplets of similar sizes and locations to the 34S hotspots can be observed in Symbiodinium cells using electron microscopy.
source: Lipid droplets of similar sizes and locations can be observed in these cells using electron microscopy (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy images shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Methionine and cysteine were not detected using LC-MS or ToF-SIMS, suggesting that the intracellular concentration of these sulfur based amino-acids was relatively low.
source: We were not able to detect methionine or cysteine using LC-MS or ToF-SIMS, which suggest that the intracellular concentration of these sulfur based amino-acids was relatively low.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of detection in analytical measurements.

claim: DMSP is by far the most abundant organic sulfur compound present in dinoflagellate cells, representing more than 50% of the total organic sulfur.
source: In contrast, DMSP is known to be by far the most abundant organic sulfur compound present in dinoflagellate cells (Matrai and Keller, 1994), representing more than 50% of the total organic sulfur in these organisms (Matrai and Keller, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Matrai and Keller, 1994.

claim: DMSP was the only organic sulfur compound detected in the Symbiodinium cells through LC-MS, 1H NMR and ToF-SIMS.
source: DMSP was the only organic sulfur compound we were able to detect in the Symbiodinium cells (through LC-MS, 1H NMR and ToF-SIMS), suggesting that most of the remaining 34S signal measured in Symbiodinium cells with NanoSIMS is highly likely originating from DMSP.
evidence: This claim is based on the analytical measurements performed in the study.

claim: Most of the 34S signal measured in Symbiodinium cells with NanoSIMS is highly likely originating from DMSP.
source: DMSP was the only organic sulfur compound we were able to detect in the Symbiodinium cells (through LC-MS, 1H NMR and ToF-SIMS), suggesting that most of the remaining 34S signal measured in Symbiodinium cells with NanoSIMS is highly likely originating from DMSP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analytical data showing DMSP as the only detectable organic sulfur compound.

claim: DMSP is an effective scavenger of reactive oxygen species (ROS), particularly hydroxyl radicals (•OH).
source: DMSP is an effective scavenger of reactive oxygen species (ROS), particularly hydroxyl radicals (•OH) (Sunda et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sunda et al., 2002.

claim: The in vivo half-life of hydroxyl radicals (•OH) is 10−9 seconds.
source: The in vivo half-life of •OH is 10−9 seconds (Sies, 1993), which implies that these highly reactive molecules can damage lipids, nucleic acids, amino-acids or carbohydrates present in their direct vicinity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sies, 1993.

claim: Hydroxyl radicals can damage lipids, nucleic acids, amino-acids or carbohydrates present in their direct vicinity.
source: The in vivo half-life of •OH is 10−9 seconds (Sies, 1993), which implies that these highly reactive molecules can damage lipids, nucleic acids, amino-acids or carbohydrates present in their direct vicinity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the short half-life of hydroxyl radicals and their reactivity.

claim: To be an effective antioxidant, a molecule needs to be able to scavenge ROS and to be located close to their source.
source: To be an effective antioxidant, a molecule needs not only to be able to scavenge ROS, but also to be located close to their source.
evidence: This is a general principle of antioxidant function based on established knowledge.

claim: If some DMSP is located in the cytoplasm, it will be ideally localised to act as an osmolyte.
source: If some DMSP is located in the cytoplasm, as suggested by our NanoSIMS data, it will be ideally localised to act as an osmolyte (Kiene et al., 1996).
evidence: This is an inference based on the NanoSIMS data showing DMSP in the cytoplasm and a citation to Kiene et al., 1996.

claim: The presence of strong 34S signals in and around chloroplasts, where ROS are formed, supports DMSP's role as an antioxidant.
source: Furthermore, the presence of strong 34S signals in and around chloroplasts, where ROS are formed, support its role as an antioxidant (Sunda et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on the NanoSIMS data and a citation to Sunda et al., 2002.

claim: Following synthesis by phytoplankton, DMSP constitutes an important carbon and sulfur source for heterotrophic marine bacteria.
source: Following synthesis by phytoplankton, DMSP constitutes an important carbon and sulfur source for heterotrophic marine bacteria, which can either demethylate the compound and incorporate its sulfur into proteins or cleave it to produce DMS (Curson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Curson et al., 2011.

claim: Marine bacteria can either demethylate DMSP and incorporate its sulfur into proteins or cleave it to produce DMS.
source: Following synthesis by phytoplankton, DMSP constitutes an important carbon and sulfur source for heterotrophic marine bacteria, which can either demethylate the compound and incorporate its sulfur into proteins or cleave it to produce DMS (Curson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Curson et al., 2011.

claim: Total DMSP concentrations in Symbiodinium cells inoculated with the DMSP-degrading bacterium Pseudovibrio sp. P12 were 31% lower relative to those containing no bacteria or bacteria unable to degrade DMSP.
source: At the termination of the experiment, total DMSP concentrations in Symbiodinium cells inoculated with the DMSP-degrading bacterium Pseudovibrio sp. P12 were 31% lower relative to those containing no bacteria or bacteria unable to degrade DMSP (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by DMSP concentration data shown in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: The lower DMSP concentrations recorded in Pseudovibrio-inoculated treatments are likely a consequence of the presence of Pseudovibrio cells able to degrade this compound.
source: As Symbiodinium abundance did not differ between the treatments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), the lower DMSP concentrations recorded are likely a consequence of the presence of Pseudovibrio cells able to degrade this compound.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DMSP concentration data and cell count data.

claim: The genome of Pseudovibrio sp. P12 was sequenced, revealing that this bacterium harbours a complete DMSP cleavage pathway.
source: We sequenced the genome of Pseudovibrio sp. P12, revealing that this bacterium harbours a complete DMSP cleavage pathway, including a DMSP acyl-CoA transferase (encoded by dddD), a DMSP transporter (dddT) and the downstream catabolic enzymes (dddB-C) (Todd et al., 2007; Raina et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequencing data and citations to previous research.

claim: Pseudovibrio sp. P12 harbours a DMSP acyl-CoA transferase (encoded by dddD), a DMSP transporter (dddT) and the downstream catabolic enzymes (dddB-C).
source: We sequenced the genome of Pseudovibrio sp. P12, revealing that this bacterium harbours a complete DMSP cleavage pathway, including a DMSP acyl-CoA transferase (encoded by dddD), a DMSP transporter (dddT) and the downstream catabolic enzymes (dddB-C) (Todd et al., 2007; Raina et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequencing data and citations to previous research.

claim: NMR analyses revealed that the DMSP degradation pathway in Pseudovibrio sp. P12 was functional, enabling this strain to convert high concentrations of DMSP into DMS.
source: Further analyses using NMR revealed that this DMSP degradation pathway was functional, enabling this strain to convert high concentrations of DMSP into DMS (Raina et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data and a citation to Raina et al., 2016.

claim: Pseudovibrio sp. P12 harbours homologues of genes involved in the demethylation pathway (dmdA-B-C-D), though these genes have relatively low sequence identity (24%, 30%, 43% and 32%, respectively) to the genes originally identified in Ruegeria pomeroyi DSS-3.
source: In addition, Pseudovibrio sp. P12 harbours homologues of genes involved in the demethylation pathway (dmdA-B-C-D), though these genes have a relatively low sequence identity (24%, 30%, 43% and 32%, respectively) (Raina et al., 2016) to the genes originally identified in Ruegeria pomeroyi DSS-3 (Reisch et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequencing data and citations to previous research.

claim: Bacteria-sized 15N hotspots localised outside Symbiodinium cells in NanoSIMS images were accurately identified as inoculated bacterial cells based on their unique nitrogen isotopic signatures (1151-fold increase on average over natural abundance, n = 79).
